newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Asia stocks mostly higher, Hang Seng hits 12,000.
newsitem.headline: Asia stocks mostly higher, Hang Seng hits 12,000.

text.p: Hong Kong stocks were mostly higher on Thursday, with the Hang Seng Index temporarily surpassing a key technical level of 12,000 points, driven by overnight records on Wall Street and in London.

But the momentum soon faded, as investors took a breather from the recent advance. The Hang Seng Index hit 12,004.33 shortly after the opening, soaring above 12,000 mark for the first time since February 4, 1994, when it hit a high of 12,186.80.
But the market started to retreat later on Thursday, falling below Wednesday's close, before advancing again to stand 33.97 points, or 0.28 percent, higher at 11,985.85 points by the lunch break.
"I'm still bullish on the market, but I think it has risen too fast. It should consolidate at this level," said Priscilla Ng, executive director at CEF GC Brokerage.
"We are likely to see the market consolidate at this level," said Francis Wu, institutional sales manager at South China Securities.
"The market is not that strong this morning," he added.
Over the longer-term, analysts remain optimistic, in part because of the favourable interest rate environment in the U.S.
"I expect to see the market continue to move ahead on the back of new highs in foreign markets...," said Anthony Mak, sales director at Vickers Ballas.
The Hang Seng London reference index hit a record 11,966.75 on Wednesday before closing at 11,965.39, up 13.51 points.
London and New York markets have set new highs as they reap the benefits of America's current interest rate policy.

On Wednesday, the Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 29.07 points to 5,933.97, surpassing the previous record of 5,905 set on Tuesday. The Dow only pierced 5,900 on Tuesday and dealers were placing wagers on when it would hit 6,000.

In London, the FTSE-100 broke the 4,000 level for the first time to set a record for the second straight day. Blue-chip stocks rallied, spurred by a strong international bond market and strength on Wall Street.
The FTSE-100 ended at 4,015.1, up 22.9 points.
Wall Street's gains gave an initial boost to Tokyo shares, but that support soon evaporated. The Nikkei 225-share index was off 139.65 points, or 0.65 percent, at 21,358.95.
"The gains at the opening lacked power, and the turnover was slim," said Kenichi Sagami, general manager at the stock department of Yamaichi Securities Co Ltd.
Traders said a weaker yen, which has resulted from the U.S. dollar's advance to a 32-month high of 112 yen, has boosted some stocks, including autos such as Honda Motor Co Ltd.
Elsewhere, Taiwan stocks rallied after the government decided not to raise the business income tax. The weighted index ended up 73.34 points, or 1.12 percent, at 6,611.58.
Thai stocks remained pressured by political concerns and were off 31.71 points, or three percent, at 1,026.97.
Malaysian shares gained 11.25 points, or 0.99 percent, to 1,150.57 and Indonesia shares were up on speculative buying. The Jakarta Composite Index was 1.4 points, or 0.24 percent, higher at 590.712.
Singapore traders ignored Wall Street's gains, leaving the Straits Times Industrials Index down 9.20 points, or 0.43 percent, at 2,153.69.
In the Philippines, stocks lost 41.62 points, or 1.31 percent, to stand at 3,130.26 as foreign fund managers moved their investments elsewhere.
Australia's All Ordinaries Index was up 12.8 points, or 0.55 percent, at 2,327.4, while New Zealand shares gained 14.38 points, or 0.65 percent, to 2,235.73.
